question: Why must an Archer II (PA-28-181) pilot verify the handbook against the individual airplane?
answer: This deck uses the archived VB-1120 handbook. The airplane’s approved, current handbook, equipment supplements, placards, and loading records determine its actual limitations and procedures. The handbook also does not replace instruction or applicable regulations.

question: What engine and propeller arrangement does this Archer II (PA-28-181) handbook describe?
answer: A four-cylinder, air-cooled, horizontally opposed Lycoming O-360-A4M or O-360-A4A driving a two-blade, fixed-pitch Sensenich propeller. This is a carbureted installation; do not substitute Archer TX or other model procedures.

question: What is VNE for the Archer II (PA-28-181) in VB-1120?
answer: 154 KIAS. This is the never-exceed speed; the red line is an operating limit, not a target to approach in turbulence or a descent.

question: What does the Archer II (PA-28-181) yellow airspeed arc require?
answer: The yellow arc is 125–154 KIAS. Above the 125-KIAS maximum structural cruising speed, operate only in smooth air and with caution; 154 KIAS remains the never-exceed limit.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §§2.3–2.5, printed pp.2-1–2-2

question: How does maneuvering speed change with weight in the Archer II (PA-28-181)?
answer: It decreases as weight decreases: VB-1120 lists 113 KIAS at 2,550 lb and 89 KIAS at 1,634 lb, with straight-line interpolation between them. Use the value appropriate to the actual weight; the gross-weight value is not suitable for every loading.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §2.3, printed p.2-2

question: What is the Archer II (PA-28-181) maximum flap-extended speed?
answer: 102 KIAS. Slow to at or below this speed before extending flaps and remain within it while they are extended.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §2.3, printed p.2-2

question: What does the white arc show on the Archer II (PA-28-181) airspeed indicator?
answer: 49–102 KIAS in this handbook. It identifies the flap operating range, from the marked landing-configuration stall speed to the maximum flap-extended speed; actual stall behavior still depends on loading and maneuvering.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §2.5, printed p.2-2

question: How do maximum ramp and takeoff weights differ for an Archer II (PA-28-181) in the normal category?
answer: Maximum ramp weight is 2,558 lb; the maximum weight for flight is 2,550 lb. Fuel used before takeoff must bring the airplane within the flight limit; a ramp allowance does not permit an overweight takeoff.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §2.11, printed p.2-4

question: What loading restrictions apply when operating the Archer II (PA-28-181) in the utility category?
answer: The handbook lists a 2,130-lb maximum flight weight and no baggage. The utility center-of-gravity envelope also applies; meeting only the weight limit is insufficient.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §§2.11–2.13, printed pp.2-4–2-5

question: Does staying below 200 lb in the Archer II (PA-28-181) baggage area guarantee legal loading?
answer: No. Two hundred pounds is the normal-category baggage limit, but total weight and center of gravity must also remain in the approved envelope. Secure the load to the baggage tie-downs.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §7.27, printed p.7-20; §2.11, printed p.2-4

question: Are intentional spins allowed in an Archer II (PA-28-181) operated in the utility category?
answer: No. The handbook prohibits intentional spins in this airplane. Utility-category approval is not permission to perform every aerobatic maneuver.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §3.25, printed p.3-15; §2.15, printed p.2-6

question: Is the Archer II (PA-28-181) automatically approved for IFR flight or flight in icing?
answer: The handbook permits day/night VFR and IFR only when the airplane is properly equipped for that operation. Its approval is for non-icing conditions; IFR capability does not provide icing approval.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §2.19, printed p.2-6

question: How much fuel can the standard Archer II (PA-28-181) fuel system actually use?
answer: It holds 50 US gallons total, with 48 usable: 24 usable gallons in each wing tank and 1 unusable gallon in each tank. Plan endurance with usable fuel, not total capacity.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §2.21, printed p.2-6

question: How much usable fuel is indicated by filling both Archer II (PA-28-181) tanks to the bottom of their filler-neck tabs?
answer: 17 US gallons usable per tank, or 34 usable gallons total. Those tab figures are not the 48-gallon full-tank usable capacity.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §7.13, printed p.7-7

question: What aviation gasoline grades are listed in the Archer II (PA-28-181) basic handbook?
answer: Grade 100 (green) or 100LL (blue). Do not assume that a fuel approval or STC on another Archer also applies to your airplane; verify its current approved documents.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §1.7, printed p.1-3

question: Why does the Archer II (PA-28-181) have an electric fuel pump as well as an engine-driven pump?
answer: The electric pump backs up the engine-driven pump. The handbook calls for it during takeoff and landing and when changing tanks, so fuel delivery has added protection during those operations.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §7.13, printed p.7-7

question: How should an Archer II (PA-28-181) pilot protect fuel flow during a tank change?
answer: Turn the electric fuel pump on before changing tanks and leave it on briefly afterward. Select a tank containing fuel and monitor engine operation and fuel pressure. The handbook cautions against intentionally running a tank dry in flight.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §4.27, printed p.4-18

question: Which Archer II (PA-28-181) fuel drains need attention before the first flight of the day?
answer: Drain and inspect samples from both wing-tank drains and the fuel-strainer drain for water, sediment, and correct fuel. The strainer drain is accessible outside near the lower left front of the firewall.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §7.13, printed p.7-8

question: What electrical supply does the Archer II (PA-28-181) basic system use?
answer: A 14-volt, 60-amp alternator and a 12-volt battery. The alternator normally supplies the airplane’s electrical demand; battery capacity becomes important if alternator output is lost.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §7.15, printed p.7-9

question: What does the Archer II (PA-28-181) ammeter actually display?
answer: It is a loadmeter: it displays current supplied by the alternator. It does not directly show battery charge or discharge, so interpret a low reading in light of the electrical load and other indications.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §7.15, printed p.7-12

question: Does an ALT warning light alone prove alternator failure in the Archer II (PA-28-181)?
answer: No. Cross-check the ammeter. The handbook notes that a very light electrical load with a fully charged battery can illuminate the warning even with a working alternator; its diagnostic check uses an added electrical load and the resulting indication.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §7.15, printed p.7-10; §3.23, printed p.3-6

question: What is the Archer II (PA-28-181) electrical situation if alternator output cannot be restored?
answer: The battery is supplying the electrical equipment. Follow the applicable failure checklist, keep electrical demand to a minimum, and land as soon as practical; the handbook does not promise a fixed battery endurance.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §3.23, printed p.3-13

question: In the Archer II (PA-28-181) conventional instrument installation, which gyros use vacuum and which instrument uses electrical power?
answer: The attitude and directional gyros use the engine-driven vacuum system. The turn-and-slip indicator or turn coordinator uses electrical power. Verify the actual installation, especially if instruments have been replaced.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §§7.17–7.19, printed p.7-14

question: Why is a falling vacuum indication important in the Archer II (PA-28-181)?
answer: Vacuum-powered attitude and heading indications may become unreliable. A zero reading can reflect a pump, gauge, or line problem, so cross-check independent instruments and follow the appropriate instrument-failure procedures.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §7.17, printed p.7-13

question: Where is the Archer II (PA-28-181) pitot-static head, and which instruments depend on it?
answer: It is beneath the left wing. The system supplies the airspeed indicator, altimeter, and vertical-speed indicator; verify that the cover is removed and the openings are clear before flight.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §7.21, printed p.7-16

question: What changes when the Archer II (PA-28-181) optional alternate static source is selected?
answer: The instruments use cabin pressure instead of the normal external static source. Follow the handbook’s cabin-configuration instructions and any applicable placarded corrections, because indications can change.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §7.21, printed p.7-16

question: Does optional pitot heat make an Archer II (PA-28-181) suitable for icing flight?
answer: No. It heats the pitot head; it does not change the handbook’s non-icing limitation or protect the airplane’s other exposed surfaces and systems.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §7.21, printed p.7-16; §2.19, printed p.2-6

question: How is pitch control arranged on the Archer II (PA-28-181)?
answer: It uses an all-moving stabilator with a trailing-edge trim tab. The pitch-trim wheel is on the floor between the front seats; include correct trim setting and free control movement in preflight checks.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §7.9, printed p.7-5

question: How are the Archer II (PA-28-181) flaps operated, and what are their extension settings?
answer: They are operated manually by the lever between the front seats, with extended settings of 10°, 25°, and 40°. They are spring-loaded toward the retracted position.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §7.9, printed p.7-5

sourceMetadata.verificationStatus: Handbook section checked; applicability limited to cited edition

question: When may the right flap be used as a step on an Archer II (PA-28-181)?
answer: Only when fully retracted, when its over-center mechanism locks it to support weight. Warn passengers before boarding or leaving the airplane.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §7.9, printed p.7-5

question: Do the Archer II (PA-28-181) toe brakes and hand brake have completely separate fluid supplies?
answer: No. Their master cylinders use a common brake-fluid reservoir. A shared fluid problem can therefore affect more than one brake control.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §7.7, printed p.7-3

question: What landing-gear arrangement should an Archer II (PA-28-181) pilot inspect?
answer: Fixed tricycle landing gear with air-oil struts on all three wheels. Check the struts, tires, brakes, and nosewheel steering condition; there is no normal landing-gear retraction procedure.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §7.7, printed p.7-3

question: How does the Archer II (PA-28-181) stall warning work, and how is it checked?
answer: An electrically powered continuous horn is triggered by a lift detector on the left wing’s leading edge, nominally 5–10 knots before the stall. With electrical power on during preflight, lift the detector vane and listen for the horn.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §7.29, printed p.7-20

question: What should an Archer II (PA-28-181) pilot check about the shoulder harness before takeoff?
answer: For an inertia-reel harness, check that a sharp pull locks the reel. With a fixed harness, adjust it so the occupant is restrained while still able to reach essential controls, including the fuel selector, flaps, and trim.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §7.25, printed p.7-20; §4.31, printed p.4-19

question: Where does the Archer II (PA-28-181) cabin-heating air get its heat?
answer: From a heater muff around the exhaust system; the warmed air also supplies the defroster. This differs from the separate fresh-air ventilation supplied through the wing-root inlets.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §7.23, printed p.7-19

question: What magneto-check results does the Archer II (PA-28-181) handbook require during run-up?
answer: At 2,000 RPM, no more than a 175-RPM drop on either magneto and no more than a 50-RPM difference between them. Each single-magneto check should last no more than 10 seconds.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §4.19, printed p.4-15

sourceMetadata.verificationStatus: Handbook section checked; applicability limited to cited edition

question: Why should an Archer II (PA-28-181) avoid prolonged ground running with carburetor heat on?
answer: The heated intake air is unfiltered. Check that carburetor heat works and clear any ice as the handbook directs, but avoid unnecessary exposure to dust or loose material on the ground.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §4.19, printed p.4-15

sourceMetadata.verificationStatus: Handbook section checked; applicability limited to cited edition

question: Why does the Archer II (PA-28-181) ground check include operating with the electric fuel pump off?
answer: It verifies that the engine-driven fuel pump can supply the engine. The electric pump is then turned back on before takeoff to provide backup during that critical phase.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §4.19, printed p.4-15

sourceMetadata.verificationStatus: Handbook section checked; applicability limited to cited edition

question: What best-rate and best-angle climb speeds are listed at gross weight for the Archer II (PA-28-181)?
answer: Best rate is 76 KIAS and best angle is 64 KIAS. The handbook says these speeds decrease somewhat at lighter weights; use the applicable aircraft handbook and performance information.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §4.25, printed p.4-17

question: Why does the Archer II (PA-28-181) handbook recommend 87 KIAS for an en route climb?
answer: It improves forward progress and visibility over the nose compared with the slower maximum-performance climb speeds. Choose the climb technique appropriate to obstacles and the actual operating conditions.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §4.25, printed p.4-17

sourceMetadata.verificationStatus: Handbook section checked; applicability limited to cited edition

question: Why is there a range of normal takeoff rotation speeds for the Archer II (PA-28-181)?
answer: Rotation depends on weight. VB-1120 describes accelerating to 48–53 KIAS, depending on loading, before easing into the climb attitude. Do not treat one end of the range as appropriate for every takeoff.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §4.23, printed p.4-17

sourceMetadata.verificationStatus: Handbook section checked; applicability limited to cited edition

question: What flap setting does the Archer II (PA-28-181) handbook use for short-field obstacle or soft-field takeoff procedures?
answer: 25°, the second notch. The associated weight-dependent speeds, acceleration, obstacle clearance, and gradual flap retraction are part of the procedure; the flap setting alone does not guarantee the charted performance.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §4.23, printed p.4-17

question: What cruise-power and mixture guidance does this Archer II (PA-28-181) handbook give?
answer: Normal maximum cruise power is 75%. It calls for leaning in cruise above 5,000 ft and permits leaning lower at 75% power or less. If power is uncertain below 5,000 ft, it directs full rich. Use the installed engine’s current approved guidance.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §4.27, printed pp.4-17–4-18

question: Why should an Archer II (PA-28-181) pilot alternate fuel use between wing tanks?
answer: To keep the airplane in good lateral trim. Manage tank changes deliberately, track remaining fuel in each tank, and do not run tanks completely dry; total fuel alone does not describe the fuel immediately available from the selected tank.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §4.27, printed p.4-18

sourceMetadata.verificationStatus: Handbook section checked; applicability limited to cited edition

question: What normal approach speeds are described for the Archer II (PA-28-181) in VB-1120?
answer: About 75 KIAS initially, then 66 KIAS on final with flaps extended. Loading, wind, runway conditions, and the applicable technique still matter; these figures are not a substitute for the full landing procedure.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §4.31, printed p.4-19

question: Does this Archer II (PA-28-181) handbook call for carburetor heat on every normal landing approach?
answer: No. It directs its use when carburetor icing is indicated and warns that the power reduction can matter during a go-around. Do not transfer an automatic carburetor-heat habit from another airplane without checking this airplane’s procedure.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §4.31, printed p.4-19

question: How is the Archer II (PA-28-181) engine normally stopped?
answer: The handbook uses the mixture control at idle cut-off to stop the engine, followed by ignition and master switches off. Follow the complete shutdown procedure, including turning off the specified electrical equipment.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §4.33, printed p.4-20

question: What is the Archer II (PA-28-181) priority after power loss immediately after takeoff?
answer: Maintain a safe airspeed and use the landing area available. If enough runway remains, land straight ahead; otherwise the handbook allows only a shallow turn as needed to avoid obstacles. Attempt restart actions only if altitude permits.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §3.9, printed p.3-9

question: What glide speed is specified for an Archer II (PA-28-181) after an engine failure at altitude?
answer: 76 KIAS for best gliding angle, with the optional air conditioner off. Establish the glide and identify a suitable landing area while using the applicable emergency checklist.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §3.13, printed p.3-11

question: Why might Archer II (PA-28-181) engine power not return immediately after switching away from an empty tank?
answer: Empty fuel lines must refill. The handbook says restoration can take up to about 10 seconds; keep flying the airplane and preparing to land rather than assuming an immediate restart.

question: What may be an early indication of carburetor ice in the fixed-pitch Archer II (PA-28-181)?
answer: A falling RPM, possibly with roughness and loss of airspeed or altitude. Act promptly using the carburetor-icing procedure; waiting for severe roughness can allow substantial ice to accumulate.

question: Why can an Archer II (PA-28-181) run rougher briefly when carburetor heat is first applied to remove ice?
answer: The handbook warns of an initial RPM reduction and increased roughness. Improvement in smoothness or a later RPM increase can indicate ice clearing; follow the full procedure instead of immediately removing heat just because of the initial response.

question: How seriously should an Archer II (PA-28-181) pilot treat loss of oil pressure?
answer: It may indicate an engine-threatening oil loss even if a gauge fault is possible. Follow the checklist, proceed toward a landing, and prepare for sudden power loss; accompanying temperature rise or oil smoke strengthens concern about an actual failure.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §3.17, printed p.3-12

question: What does the Archer II (PA-28-181) handbook direct for loss of fuel pressure?
answer: Turn on the electric fuel pump and verify selection of a tank containing fuel. If an empty tank is not the cause, land as soon as practical and have the engine-driven pump and fuel system checked.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §3.19, printed p.3-13

question: What should a rapid, steady oil-temperature rise prompt in an Archer II (PA-28-181)?
answer: Treat it as a sign of trouble. Watch oil pressure, follow the high-temperature procedure, and land at the nearest airport for investigation rather than continuing simply because the engine still runs.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §3.21, printed p.3-13

question: If the Archer II (PA-28-181) cabin door opens partially just after takeoff, is an immediate abrupt maneuver necessary?
answer: No. The handbook says a partially open door does not alter normal flight characteristics and a normal landing can be made. Fly the airplane first; use the door procedure when workload and conditions permit.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §3.27, printed p.3-15

question: Why must an Archer II (PA-28-181) pilot distinguish an electrical fire from an engine fire?
answer: The isolation actions differ. The electrical-fire procedure removes electrical power; the engine-fire procedure stops fuel flow and prepares for a power-off landing. Identify the likely source while following the applicable emergency checklist and landing promptly.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §3.15, printed pp.3-11–3-12

question: Do Archer II (PA-28-181) performance charts already include a safety allowance for pilot technique or aircraft deterioration?
answer: No. The handbook calls the charts unfactored: they do not allow for reduced pilot proficiency or mechanical deterioration. Match the chart technique and conditions, then add an appropriate operating margin.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §5.3, printed p.5-1

question: Can the Archer II (PA-28-181) landing-distance chart be used unchanged for a wet or grass runway?
answer: No. The landing chart specifies a paved, level, dry runway and its stated technique. Conditions outside those assumptions require additional evaluation; the basic chart is not a wet- or grass-runway performance guarantee.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §5.7, Figure 5-35, printed p.5-28; §5.3, printed p.5-1

question: Which empty-weight figures should an Archer II (PA-28-181) pilot use before deciding how much fuel or baggage to load?
answer: Use the individual airplane’s current basic empty weight and center of gravity, including equipment changes. Add occupants, usable fuel, and baggage, then check both weight and CG limits; a sample loading or another Archer’s records are insufficient.

question: The Archer II (PA-28-181) fuel gauges look adequate, but a visual tank check shows less fuel than expected. Which information should control the departure decision?
answer: Resolve the discrepancy before departure and plan from a verified usable quantity. The preflight requires both a gauge check and a visual check of each tank’s supply and fuel color; a reassuring gauge reading does not replace looking in the tanks.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §4.9, printed p.4-10

question: After refueling an Archer II (PA-28-181), is one fuel-strainer sample with the selector left on one tank the complete POH contamination check?
answer: No. The amplified preflight calls for draining both tank sumps first, then the strainer with each tank selected in turn. Examine the collected fuel and confirm that each drain closes without leaking. This check is required after refueling as well as before the day’s first flight.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §4.9, printed p.4-11

question: During a cold start, the Archer II (PA-28-181) engine has not fired after 5–10 seconds. Should the pilot simply keep the starter engaged?
answer: No. The handbook directs disengaging the starter, priming, and repeating the starting procedure. Reassess the engine’s condition and use the applicable starting procedure instead of prolonged continuous cranking.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §4.13(a), printed p.4-13

question: An Archer II (PA-28-181) engine is flooded. Why would continuing a rich-mixture start with the electric fuel pump on be the wrong approach?
answer: It continues supplying fuel when the flooded-start procedure instead calls for the pump off, mixture at idle cut-off, and throttle open during cranking. Once the engine fires, mixture and throttle must be adjusted promptly. Use the complete flooded-start procedure for the installed airplane.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §4.13(c), printed p.4-13

question: An Archer II (PA-28-181) starts successfully using optional Piper External Power, but shows no alternator output afterward. Is that enough to depart?
answer: No. A successful external-power start does not establish that the charging system works. After disconnecting the external supply and selecting the master on, the handbook requires an alternator-output check and specifically rules out flight with no output indication.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §4.13(d), printed p.4-13

question: The Archer II (PA-28-181) has completed its normal warm-up time, but the engine skips or oil pressure drops when the throttle is opened. Is elapsed warm-up time enough for takeoff?
answer: No. The warm-up guidance makes satisfactory throttle response and oil pressure part of readiness for takeoff. Investigate the abnormal response before departing; waiting a prescribed number of minutes alone does not make an engine ready.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §4.15, printed p.4-14

question: The Archer II (PA-28-181) rolls normally out of parking, but its initial taxi brake check is ineffective. Should the pilot continue to run-up to investigate there?
answer: No. Stop safely and resolve the problem before continuing. The POH calls for testing the brakes after moving only a few feet and checking steering with gentle turns, so a defect is discovered before normal taxi speeds or confined areas increase the risk.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §4.17, printed p.4-15

question: An Archer II (PA-28-181) develops an induction fire during an overprimed start. Should the pilot keep priming to help it start?
answer: No. Use the engine-fire-during-start procedure, which attempts to draw the fire into the engine rather than add fuel. If it persists beyond a few seconds, external extinguishing action is needed; the procedure calls for fuel shutoff and idle cut-off when using external extinguishing means.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §3.7, printed p.3-9

question: After the Archer II (PA-28-181) rough-engine checks, the engine runs satisfactorily on one magneto but not on BOTH. Does that justify continuing the planned trip?
answer: No. The handbook directs proceeding on the satisfactory magneto at reduced power, with mixture full rich, to the first available airport. A usable magneto can support a landing decision; it does not resolve the ignition fault.

question: An Archer II (PA-28-181) pilot selects only a little carburetor heat to remove suspected ice while limiting power loss. What is the POH concern?
answer: Partial heat can melt some ice and allow it to refreeze farther into the intake. The handbook calls for full heat when removing carburetor ice, then full cold after the ice has cleared, using the complete icing/roughness procedure.

question: The Archer II (PA-28-181) ammeter reads 60 A although the known load is about 30 A. Why is “the alternator is rated for 60 A” an incomplete explanation?
answer: The overload procedure uses output more than 20 A above the known load, not simply output above the alternator rating. A low battery or fault may be drawing the extra current. Follow the overload procedure for the actual BAT/ALT switch arrangement; interlocked and independent switches have different instructions.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §3.24, printed p.3-14

question: After switching the Archer II (PA-28-181) master off for an electrical problem, can the pilot still rely on its normal stall-warning horn?
answer: No. The handbook states that the stall-warning system is inoperative with the master off. Maintain appropriate airspeed and angle-of-attack awareness without waiting for an electrical warning that is no longer available.

question: An air-conditioned Archer II (PA-28-181) has its A/C switch on before takeoff. Is the full-throttle automatic cutout a substitute for selecting A/C off?
answer: No. The before-takeoff procedure explicitly requires A/C off for normal takeoff performance. Full throttle normally disengages the compressor and retracts the condenser scoop, but that automatic feature does not replace the required switch selection. The A/C DOOR OPEN light refers to that condenser scoop.

question: For an Archer II (PA-28-181) landing in a strong crosswind, must the pilot use the same full-flap configuration as a normal short landing?
answer: No. The POH says that higher approach speeds with partial or no flaps may be desirable in strong crosswinds. Select a technique suited to wind, loading, and runway conditions, and reassess the landing distance rather than assuming the short-landing configuration is always best.
source: Piper Archer II PA-28-181 POH VB-1120, §4.31, printed p.4-20

question: After touchdown during an Archer II (PA-28-181) short landing, how does the POH improve braking effectiveness?
answer: It describes raising the flaps and applying aft control pressure to put more weight on the main wheels while braking. Keep directional control and positively identify the flap control; this is a ground-roll technique, not permission to retract flaps prematurely in flight.

question: During a prolonged power-off descent in the Archer II (PA-28-181), why should the pilot periodically check throttle response?
answer: The handbook calls for briefly opening and closing the throttle about every 30 seconds to clear the engine and verify response. It also calls for full carburetor heat before reducing power if icing is suspected, with mixture adjusted as required.

question: An Archer II (PA-28-181) cruise plan uses the best-power chart, but the pilot leans an optional EGT installation to peak EGT. Do those assumptions match?
answer: No. In this handbook, peak EGT is the best-economy reference; best power uses 100°F rich of peak. Use the chart and mixture procedure that match, within the permitted power/altitude conditions and current engine guidance.

question: While leaning the Archer II (PA-28-181) using optional EGT, the engine becomes rough before the gauge reaches a clear peak. Should the pilot keep leaning to force a higher indication?
answer: No. The handbook uses the EGT at the onset of roughness as the peak reference in that situation. Apply the selected approved mixture procedure from that reference instead of accepting rough operation merely to find a numerical peak.

question: In the Archer II (PA-28-181) planning example, cruise uses 19.5 gal, climb 1 gal, and descent 1 gal. Is 19.5 gal the trip fuel, and how much weight is actually burned?
answer: No. Add the segments: 21.5 US gal, or 129 lb using the handbook’s 6 lb/gal planning value. That is the example’s airborne trip burn; separately include ground use and the fuel reserve needed for the actual flight.

question: For an Archer II (PA-28-181) departing an elevated airport, the climb chart gives 11.5 min to cruise conditions and 3 min to departure-field conditions. What is the climb time for this departure?
answer: 8.5 minutes: subtract the departure-field value from the cruise-altitude value. The POH applies this same endpoint subtraction to climb distance and fuel; using the full sea-level-to-cruise amount would misstate this climb segment.

question: An Archer II (PA-28-181) route is 314 NM, with 11.5 NM allocated to climb and 20.5 NM to descent. How much distance should be assigned to cruise?
answer: 282 NM: 314 − 11.5 − 20.5. The POH plans climb, cruise, and descent separately; treating the entire route as cruise and then adding complete climb/descent segments would double-count distance.

question: For a hypothetical Archer II (PA-28-181) cruise segment of 282 NM at 110 KTAS and 7.6 GPH, what does a steady 20-kt headwind do to the cruise fuel estimate?
answer: Groundspeed becomes 90 kt. The segment takes about 3.13 hours and uses about 23.8 gal, instead of about 19.5 gal in still air. These are illustrative steady-condition calculations, excluding climb, descent, ground fuel, and reserve; use actual forecast winds and verified performance.

question: An Archer II (PA-28-181) pilot checks only landing ground roll for a runway with a 50-ft obstacle at the approach end. What performance comparison is missing?
answer: Use the landing distance over a 50-ft barrier, not just the ground roll after touchdown. VB-1120 provides separate landing-performance and ground-roll charts; compare the applicable total distance and technique with the available runway and add an operating margin.

question: An Archer II (PA-28-181) would weigh 2,300 lb at takeoff before adding usable fuel. Using 6 lb/gal, can it take off with all 48 usable gallons?
answer: No. Full usable fuel adds 288 lb, making 2,588 lb. The 2,550-lb normal-category limit leaves 250 lb, or about 41.7 usable gallons by weight alone. CG, performance, fuel reserve, and any other applicable limits may require a different loading or flight plan.

question: A hypothetical Archer II (PA-28-181) loading totals 2,400 lb and 219,000 lb-in of moment. How is its CG found, and what is the next check?
answer: Divide moment by weight: 219,000 ÷ 2,400 = 91.25 inches aft of datum. Then plot that CG with the 2,400-lb weight in the applicable category envelope; a moment calculation alone does not establish an acceptable loading.

question: An Archer II (PA-28-181) weighs 2,400 lb at a 91.0-in CG. A 150-lb passenger plans to move from the 80.5-in front-seat station to the 118.1-in rear-seat station. Is the unchanged total weight enough to approve the move?
answer: No. The move adds 150 × (118.1 − 80.5) = 5,640 lb-in of moment, moving CG aft by 2.35 in to 93.35 in. That exceeds this handbook’s 93.0-in normal-category aft limit. Use actual loading data and approved seating arrangements before changing the plan.

question: A hypothetical Archer II (PA-28-181) starts at 2,400 lb with 219,000 lb-in of moment and burns 20 gal from the standard 95-in fuel station. What happens to its CG?
answer: Using 6 lb/gal, remove 120 lb and 11,400 lb-in. The new CG is 207,600 ÷ 2,280 ≈ 91.05 in, moving forward from 91.25 in. Fuel burn changes both weight and CG; verify the loading stays inside the envelope throughout flight.

question: An Archer II (PA-28-181) departs at 2,400 lb and its planned airborne fuel burn is 129 lb. Which weight belongs in the destination landing-performance calculation?
answer: The predicted landing weight is 2,271 lb, provided the planned burn occurs and no other weight changes intervene. Use that landing weight with destination conditions, and update the calculation if actual fuel use or the destination changes.

question: An Archer II (PA-28-181) normal-category loading is 2,400 lb at an 85.0-in CG. Is it acceptable just because 85 in lies between the handbook’s overall 82- and 93-in extremes?
answer: No. The forward limit depends on weight. Interpolating from 82.0 in at 2,050 lb to 88.6 in at 2,550 lb gives about 86.62 in at 2,400 lb. An 85.0-in CG is too far forward even though total weight is below maximum.

question: An Archer II (PA-28-181) will be left outdoors overnight. Does setting its parking brake complete the POH parking precautions?
answer: No. The parking guidance also includes securing the control wheel with the belt, retracting the flaps, chocking the wheels, and securing the wing and tail tie-downs. Use the available approved tie-down points and appropriate precautions for the expected conditions.
